facts.claim: "Hey Baby" (feat. Mos Def) is a 4:55 track on Stephen Marley's debut solo album Mind Control, released March 20, 2007.
The track is credited as ℗ 2007 Universal Records, a division of UMG Recordings. Audiomack lists Damian "Jr. Gong" Marley as producer, though that listing is not corroborated elsewhere.
Reggae Report says the song was written for Marley's children. He used to sing it to them on the road, and they now consider it their song.
Reggae Report says the Mos Def rap on the track was a two-year-old rap, remixed for the album. Marley says it adds "swagger".
According to Reggae Report, "Hey Baby" is the only song on Mind Control that Stephen Marley did not write himself.

In a Glide Magazine interview about Mind Control, Marley was asked why he chose Mos Def for "Hey Baby". His answer, as excerpted, is that Mos Def is a conscious person who can bring enlightenment to a topic, and that the two are friends.
A review describes "Hey Baby" as having a bit of neo-soul sheen. On the album Marley mixes roots reggae, dancehall, hip-hop and contemporary R&B.
Stephen Marley is the second son of Bob and Rita Marley. He was a member of the Melody Makers and a producer for other artists before releasing Mind Control, his first solo album, in 2007.

Marley produced his brother Damian's albums Halfway Tree (2001) and Welcome to Jamrock (2005). He also began production work in 1996, remixing the Fugees and later working with Eve, Krayzie Bone and Erykah Badu.

Mind Control was nominated for the Reggae Grammy, with the ceremony on February 10, 2008. Its follow-ups were Mind Control Acoustic (2008), Revelation Pt. 1: The Root of Life (2011) and Revelation Pt. 2: The Fruit of Life (2016).

research.lineage: The song sits in the Marley family's roots reggae tradition, blended with hip-hop and neo-soul, and the album drew criticism from some reggae purists for that mix.

draft:
In the last choruses of **Hey Baby**, one word changes. All along, the singer has had to "bear" a cross. By the end, it has to be "bury." The weight he's been carrying out the door gets put in the ground, and the man who kept leaving finally sounds like he's coming home. It's a one-letter-off rewrite, and it holds the whole song: a promise that the long absence was worth it, made by someone who badly needs that to be true.

The opening verse is a leaving speech, and it argues with itself. "I got to do what I must do to be a better man," Stephen Marley sings, which is pride and apology in the same breath. He insists the road is how he keeps his blessings from turning into curses. He also keeps asking to be forgiven for it. Watch the plea shift between verses: first it's "please don't fuss," then "please don't cry." The person at home has gone from annoyed to hurt, and the singer knows it. He doesn't resolve that. He just keeps promising.

Read it as a love song and it works. But it was written for Marley's children. He used to sing it to them on the road, and they now call it theirs. That changes the "baby." The guilt becomes a parent's guilt, and the promise is being made to someone too young to argue back. The tender images, wind and tree, warmth of day and cool of night, start to sound like a father trying to describe a closeness he can't be there to give.

The band keeps all of this gentle. A steady, mid-tempo reggae beat lands its snare on two and four. The bass line stays simple. A clean electric guitar picks out an arpeggiated figure, and keyboards hold sustained chords underneath. The groove has a slight swing, relaxed and unhurried. The lead voice is clear with a little rasp, and a second voice shadows it in unison or a third above. That gives the chorus the feel of a family singalong. The polish is real, and it's the neo-soul sheen that put Mind Control at odds with some reggae purists. Here, though, it suits a lullaby.

Mos Def's verse was a rap he'd had for two years, remixed for the album. Marley says it adds "swagger," and he picked his friend for being a conscious voice. Mos Def brings the loneliness the singing smooths over: "And the spot is hot it's cold and lonely at nights." He's admitting the road costs the traveler too, not just the people left behind. Then he lands on the song's real comfort: every road ends, "and I'm back home again."

What sticks is how hard the song works to reassure. You can hear a parent soothing a child, and at the same time soothing himself that the leaving was worth it.
